Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Single-Row Subqueries
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Single-Row Subqueries

Use a single scalar value from an inner query to drive comparisons and enrich result rows.

16:9 HD Classroom

Single-row subqueries compute a single value you can compare with =, >, <, >=, <=, or <>. They are powerful because the comparison value is calculated at runtime. We will explore use in WHERE, HAVING, and SELECT, and practice avoiding ORA-01427 when multiple rows appear unexpectedly.

In this lesson
Definition, examples, error troubleshooting, and scalar subqueries in SELECT.
Core example
Compare salary to the average salary calculated by a subquery.
Common pitfall
Using a single-row operator when the subquery returns many rows yields ORA-01427.
Concept Map
Scalar result
Inner query returns one value that outer query can compare to a column.
Place
WHERE, HAVING, or SELECT list as a scalar subquery for contextual data.
Explore Key Topics
Avg compare
Use AVG in a subquery to compare each row to an aggregate.
Scalar in SELECT
Correlated scalar subqueries return contextual values per row.
ORA-01427
Confirm single-row output or switch to multi-row operators.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives describe the skills you will practice and why they matter. First, you will construct and execute SELECT statements that use single-row subqueries so your queries can adapt to values calculated at runtime. For example, computing the average salary in a subquery and using that value to filter rows makes your S Q L flexible and data-driven. Second, you will learn to use single-row comparison operators such as equals, greater than, less than, and not equals with subqueries. Choosing the correct operator prevents logical errors and communicates intent clearly. Third, you will identify and troubleshoot the ORA-01427 error that appears when a single-row comparison finds multiple rows. Knowing how to diagnose that error — by running the subquery on its own and confirming the result set size — helps you resolve queries quickly. Finally, you will practice applying single-row subqueries in WHERE and HAVING clauses and in the SELECT list as scalar subqueries, and you will confirm data type compatibility between the subquery result and the outer column to avoid implicit conversion problems. Each objective focuses on practical checks you can use while developing real queries.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Checks
screens.narratorSegment: These practical checks help you apply the chapter objectives safely. First, always test a subquery alone to confirm it returns exactly one row and one column when you plan a single-row comparison. This step surfaces potential ORA-01427 issues before they stop your query. Second, be mindful of data type compatibility: ensure the value returned by the subquery is implicitly convertible to the type of the outer column. For instance, comparing a numeric column to a character result can cause unexpected conversions or errors, so prefer aligned types. Third, when you suspect multiple rows may be returned, switch to multiple-row operators like IN, ANY, or ALL, or refine the subquery with aggregation or filters to force a single result. Finally, understand scalar subqueries in the SELECT list: these are correlated when they reference the outer row and must be designed with performance in mind because the inner query may run per outer row. Practice these checks as part of writing and testing queries to avoid common pitfalls.

Practical Checks

Small tests and type checks prevent the most common subquery mistakes.

01
Run the subquery first
Execute the inner query alone to confirm it returns a single value. This exposes unexpected duplicates early and avoids ORA-01427 interruptions.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

Check data types
Make sure the subquery's result type is compatible with the outer column to avoid implicit conversion surprises or errors.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

If the inner query may return many rows, prefer IN, ANY, or ALL, or aggregate or filter the subquery to one value if appropriate.

screens.title: What is a Single-Row Subquery?
screens.narratorSegment: A single-row subquery is an inner SELECT designed to return exactly one row and one column. Because it produces a single scalar value, you can use it directly with single-row comparison operators like equals, greater than, less than, and not equals. This is different from a multi-row subquery that returns many values and requires operators such as IN, ANY, or ALL. The single-row subquery is useful when the comparison depends on a value computed at runtime, such as an average or a maximum. A practical example is filtering employees whose salary is greater than the company average: the inner query computes AVG(salary) and returns one value; the outer query compares each salary to that single result. A common misconception is thinking the database will implicitly reduce multiple rows to one value; it will not. If the subquery returns multiple rows, Oracle raises ORA-01427. Another misconception is that scalar subqueries in the SELECT list behave like constant expressions; if they reference the outer query they are correlated and may execute per row. Takeaway: treat single-row subqueries as a one-by-one value provider and validate the inner query returns exactly one value before relying on it.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: A single-row subquery returns one row and one column and is used with single-row comparison operators.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › What is a Single-Row Subquery?
Definition

Single-row subquery

An inner SELECT that returns one row and one column. Because it yields a scalar, it pairs with single-row comparison operators in the outer query.

When to use it
When an outer comparison depends on a single computed value like AVG or MAX.
Common misconception
Assuming multiple rows will be auto-reduced to one; Oracle will raise ORA-01427 instead.
Concrete example
-- Find all employees whose salary is greater than the company's average salary.
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (
    SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees
);
Why it matters
You compute comparison values dynamically, keeping queries accurate as data changes.
Key Takeaway
Validate the inner query returns a single scalar before using single-row operators.

screens.title: How the Database Evaluates a Single-Row Subquery
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the execution order clarifies why an inner calculation can drive an outer comparison. Oracle evaluates the subquery first if it does not depend on the outer row, producing a single scalar result. That scalar is then used in the outer WHERE or HAVING comparison as if you had hard-coded the value. For correlated scalar subqueries placed in the SELECT list, the inner query references the outer row and therefore executes once per outer row; this produces a contextual value for each returned row. A concrete example is computing the department average inside a correlated subquery in the SELECT list: for every employee row, the inner query computes AVG(salary) for that employee's department. A common misconception is to assume correlated scalars are free — they can be expensive because of repeated execution. Walkthrough steps: 1) Run and inspect the inner query alone to confirm shape. 2) If independent, let the database compute it once and substitute the scalar. 3) If correlated, be aware of the per-row cost and consider a join or analytic function alternative. Reflect: are you getting a single scalar or will the inner logic run many times?

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › How the Database Evaluates
Execution order

Evaluate inner query first

  • 1. If the subquery is independent, the engine computes a single scalar and substitutes it into the outer comparison.
  • 2. If the subquery is correlated, it references the outer row and may execute once per outer row.
  • 3. For correlated scalar subqueries in SELECT, expect higher execution counts and consider alternatives for large result sets.
Quick check
Run the inner query by itself. If it returns one row, you are safe for a single-row comparison; if it returns many, refine it or change your operator.
Example — Correlated scalar
SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.salary,
  (SELECT AVG(salary)
   FROM employees
   WHERE department_id = e.department_id) AS department_avg_salary
FROM employees e;
Misconception
Assuming correlated scalars run only once; they can run many times depending on the outer row count.
Key Takeaway
Decide between a correlated scalar and other strategies based on correctness and performance trade-offs.

screens.title: Single-Row Operators vs. Multiple-Row Alternatives
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right comparison operator stops logic problems before they occur. Single-row operators, such as equals, greater than, and less than, are correct only when the subquery returns one value. If you inadvertently use one of these while the subquery produces multiple rows, Oracle raises ORA-01427. An alternative is to use multiple-row operators: IN compares a value against a set of values, ANY and ALL allow comparisons across sets using relational operators. For example, if a subquery might return several department identifiers, the outer query should use IN instead of equals to match any of those departments. A practical habit is to run the subquery alone, inspect the number of rows, and then select the operator that matches that result shape. A common misconception is thinking that ANY and ALL are interchangeable; they are not. ANY returns true if the comparison is true for at least one value, while ALL requires the comparison to be true for every returned value. Always map the operator semantics to the intended business rule. Single-Row Operators vs. Multiple-Row Alternatives means use single-row operators only with one-value subqueries; use in, any, or all when the subquery can return multiple values.. In practical terms, when to use =, >, < and when to prefer in, any, all. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Use single-row operators only with one-value subqueries; use IN, ANY, or ALL when the subquery can return multiple values.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Single-Row Operators vs. Multiple-Row Alternatives
When to use

Single-row operators

  • Use =, >, <, >=, <=, or <> when the subquery returns one scalar value.
  • If the inner query may return multiple values, choose IN, ANY, or ALL instead.
  • Always inspect the subquery output shape before picking the operator.
Operator quick reference
IN
Match any value from a subquery result set. Use when subquery returns multiple rows to match one of them.
ANY
True if the comparison holds for at least one value returned by the subquery.
ALL
True only if the comparison holds for every value returned by the subquery.
Misconception
Using = with a multi-row subquery does not silently match one value; it raises ORA-01427.

screens.title: ORA-01427 — Cause and Diagnosis
screens.narratorSegment: ORA-01427 appears when a single-row comparison operator expects one value but the subquery returns multiple rows. The database cannot reduce multiple values to a single scalar automatically, so it reports this error. To diagnose it, run the inner query by itself exactly as written and check the number of rows it returns. If you find more than one row, determine whether to refine the subquery to a single value by adding aggregation, narrowing filters, or by returning a specific key. Alternatively, change the outer comparison to a multiple-row operator like IN, ANY, or ALL to express the intended logic. A concrete example in the chapter shows attempting to match department_id to the department_id of an employee with last name 'King' — if multiple employees share that name and belong to different departments, the subquery returns several department identifiers and ORA-01427 occurs. A common student mistake is trying to fix ORA-01427 by adding LIMIT-like clauses they are unfamiliar with in Oracle; instead, use aggregation, stricter predicates, or the appropriate multi-row operator. Final thought: knowing the shape of your subquery result is the quickest way to avoid this error.

keyIdea.title: ORA-01427
keyIdea.text: Occurs when a subquery returns multiple rows but the outer comparison expected a single row; inspect and adjust the subquery or operator.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › ORA-01427 — Cause and Diagnosis
Error cause

Single-row subquery returned many rows

Oracle raises ORA-01427 when an outer comparison expects one value but the inner query produced multiple rows. This is a shape mismatch between the expected scalar and the actual result set.

Diagnosis steps:
  1. Run the subquery alone and count the rows returned.
  2. If multiple rows exist, decide whether to aggregate, filter, or switch operators.
  3. Test the adjusted subquery independently before embedding it.
Example that fails
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name
FROM employees
WHERE department_id = (
  SELECT department_id
  FROM employees
  WHERE last_name = 'King'
);
-- Error ORA-01427 if multiple 'King' rows return different department_ids
Fix options
Aggregate, add WHERE filters to make the result unique, or change the outer comparison to IN when multiple department IDs are expected.

screens.title: Using Single-Row Subqueries in HAVING
screens.narratorSegment: Single-row subqueries also appear in HAVING clauses to filter grouped aggregates. Because HAVING evaluates after GROUP BY computes aggregates, placing a subquery that returns a single value in HAVING lets you compare group aggregates to a calculated reference. A concrete example from the chapter finds departments where the department average salary exceeds the average salary of a specific job role, such as IT programmers. The inner subquery computes AVG(salary) for IT programmers and returns one scalar. The HAVING clause then compares each department's AVG(salary) to that reference. A potential pitfall is forgetting that both sides of the comparison are aggregates: ensure the subquery is scalar and that grouping logic produces one value per department. If the inner subquery accidentally yields multiple rows, ORA-01427 will occur. Another misconception is assuming HAVING can use non-aggregated columns without GROUP BY; it cannot. Takeaway: use single-row subqueries in HAVING to compare group-level aggregates to runtime-computed reference values, and validate the inner query returns one scalar. Using Single-Row Subqueries in HAVING means having can compare a group aggregate to a scalar subquery result; ensure both sides are compatible and scalar.. In practical terms, filtering grouped results with a single scalar comparison. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: HAVING can compare a group aggregate to a scalar subquery result; ensure both sides are compatible and scalar.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Using Single-Row Subqueries in HAVING
Pattern

Compare group aggregates to a scalar

-- Find departments where dept average > avg for IT_PROG
SELECT department_id, AVG(salary) AS dept_avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING AVG(salary) > (
  SELECT AVG(salary)
  FROM employees
  WHERE job_id = 'IT_PROG'
);
Why this works
The inner AVG returns a scalar reference; HAVING compares each group's aggregate to that reference to filter departments.
Key Takeaway
Validate the inner query returns one value and that group aggregates are computed correctly before comparison.
Common mistakes
  • Using non-aggregated columns in HAVING without grouping.
  • Assuming the inner subquery will collapse duplicates automatically.
  • Neglecting type compatibility between aggregates and the subquery result.

The inner query uses AVG(salary) to compute that single reference number at runtime. When you run the inner query on its own it returns one numeric result. The outer query then compares each employee's salary to that computed average and returns only those above it. This approach is powerful because the threshold adapts to data changes without rewriting the outer S Q L. A common misconception is to believe this is slower than a precomputed constant; for stable datasets a stored threshold might save time, but the dynamic subquery guarantees correctness. To test this pattern: first run SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees; then embed it inside the WHERE clause. If the inner query unexpectedly returns more than one column or row, refine it. Closing question: is the inner query independent or correlated? Here it is independent and computed once, so this pattern is efficient for a single scalar reference. keyIdea.text: Compute AVG(salary) as a scalar subquery and compare each salary to that value in the WHERE clause.

content.html:
Module 05 › Chapter 5.2 › Example: Employees Above Average Salary
Goal

Find employees earning above the company average

-- Step 1: Test the inner query independently
SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees;

-- Step 2: Use it in the outer query
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, salary
FROM employees
WHERE salary > (
  SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees
);
Practical tip: run the inner query first to confirm it returns one numeric value. If it does, embed it and run the full query.
Explanation

Independent single-row subqueries are evaluated once and supply a reliable comparison value.

screens.title: Data Type Compatibility
screens.narratorSegment: Data type compatibility ensures the value returned by the subquery can be meaningfully compared to the outer column. If the subquery returns a number and the outer column is numeric, comparisons behave predictably. If types differ, Oracle may attempt implicit conversion, which can fail or yield unexpected results. For example, comparing a numeric column to a character result can produce errors or silent conversion that changes semantics. Best practice is to ensure the subquery returns the correct type explicitly, using CAST if necessary, or selecting matching columns from the same table. A concrete check is to run the inner query and inspect the returned data type or use a DESCRIBE on referenced columns. A common misconception is assuming Oracle will always convert types correctly; implicit conversions can hide bugs and reduce clarity. Takeaway: align types between subquery results and outer columns to prevent runtime errors and subtle logic bugs. Concept

Match types for reliable comparisons

When comparing an outer column to a scalar from a subquery, the types should be compatible. If not, implicit conversions may take place or errors may occur. Use CAST or explicit selection of a numeric expression when needed.

Practical check
Run the inner query and inspect the result. Confirm the type aligns with the column used in the outer comparison.
Misconception
Assuming implicit conversion will always preserve the intended meaning of the value; it can introduce subtle bugs.
Example
If the outer column is NUMBER and the subquery selects a VARCHAR2 column, consider using CAST(subquery_result AS NUMBER) or selecting a numeric expression to guarantee compatibility.
Key Takeaway
Align types or convert explicitly in the subquery to ensure correct comparisons and avoid surprises.

screens.title: Scalar Subqueries in the SELECT List
screens.narratorSegment: A scalar subquery in the SELECT list returns at most one value per outer row and enriches each result row with contextual information. Often these are correlated: the inner query references a column from the outer row, for example department_id, to compute an aggregate specific to that row's context. An example is adding department average salary alongside each employee row. This is powerful for reporting because each returned row carries its own computed context. However, correlated scalar subqueries may execute once per outer row, which can impact performance on large datasets. A misconception is to overuse scalar subqueries where a join or analytic function would be more efficient. When designing a report, weigh the clarity of a scalar subquery against potential performance costs. If you rely on a scalar subquery, confirm it returns at most one row per outer row; if it returns multiple rows, ORA-01427 will trigger for that row. Final takeaway: scalar subqueries are excellent for contextual fields but should be used judiciously when result counts are large. Pattern

Correlated scalar example

SELECT e.employee_id, e.first_name, e.last_name, e.salary,
(SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employees WHERE department_id = e.department_id) AS department_avg_salary
FROM employees e;
This inner query depends on e.department_id and produces one average per department for each outer row. Validate it returns a single scalar per outer row to avoid errors.
Considerations

Use scalar subqueries to add context, but profile performance and consider set-based alternatives for large tables.

Retrieve employee details for the highest salary

screens.title: Debugging and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Effective debugging of single-row subqueries follows a small set of practical steps. First, run the subquery on its own to confirm shape and value. Second, verify the returned data type and convert explicitly if necessary. Third, if the subquery returns multiple rows but your intent is a single value, either refine the WHERE clause or apply aggregation to reduce it to one result. Fourth, when using correlated scalar subqueries, consider whether a join, GROUP BY, or analytic function achieves the same result with better performance. A common student mistake is to reflexively place scalar subqueries everywhere for clarity, ignoring performance at scale. Another is to assume errors like ORA-01427 always mean the outer logic is wrong — often the inner query simply returned more rows than expected. For performance, run an EXPLAIN PLAN and profile queries if you suspect repeated inner executions. Finally, document your intent in comments so future maintainers understand why a scalar subquery was chosen instead of a join. Closing question: which approach gives the best balance of clarity and performance for your use case? fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we will learn how to build and use single-row subqueries — those that return exactly one row and one column. You will understand why these subqueries are useful for dynamic comparisons, how they appear in WHERE and HAVING clauses, how to use them as scalar subqueries in a SELECT list, and how to avoid the common ORA-01427 error when multiple rows are returned. For example, you will see how an inner query can compute an average salary at runtime, and how the outer query compares each employee's salary to that single computed value. We will also cover data type compatibility so your comparisons behave predictably, and we will practice a hands-on activity to find employees with the highest salary using a MAX subquery. By the end of this lesson you will be able to pick the right comparison operator, confirm a subquery returns a single value, and convert a conceptual requirement into a safe and correct SELECT statement. As you work through examples, notice the difference between a scalar result and a multi-row result, and ask yourself whether the comparison operator you plan to use expects one value or many.

These objectives describe the skills you will practice and why they matter. First, you will construct and execute SELECT statements that use single-row subqueries so your queries can adapt to values calculated at runtime. For example, computing the average salary in a subquery and using that value to filter rows makes your S Q L flexible and data-driven. Second, you will learn to use single-row comparison operators such as equals, greater than, less than, and not equals with subqueries. Choosing the correct operator prevents logical errors and communicates intent clearly. Third, you will identify and troubleshoot the ORA-01427 error that appears when a single-row comparison finds multiple rows. Knowing how to diagnose that error — by running the subquery on its own and confirming the result set size — helps you resolve queries quickly. Finally, you will practice applying single-row subqueries in WHERE and HAVING clauses and in the SELECT list as scalar subqueries, and you will confirm data type compatibility between the subquery result and the outer column to avoid implicit conversion problems. Each objective focuses on practical checks you can use while developing real queries.

These practical checks help you apply the chapter objectives safely. First, always test a subquery alone to confirm it returns exactly one row and one column when you plan a single-row comparison. This step surfaces potential ORA-01427 issues before they stop your query. Second, be mindful of data type compatibility: ensure the value returned by the subquery is implicitly convertible to the type of the outer column. For instance, comparing a numeric column to a character result can cause unexpected conversions or errors, so prefer aligned types. Third, when you suspect multiple rows may be returned, switch to multiple-row operators like IN, ANY, or ALL, or refine the subquery with aggregation or filters to force a single result. Finally, understand scalar subqueries in the SELECT list: these are correlated when they reference the outer row and must be designed with performance in mind because the inner query may run per outer row. Practice these checks as part of writing and testing queries to avoid common pitfalls.

A single-row subquery is an inner SELECT designed to return exactly one row and one column. Because it produces a single scalar value, you can use it directly with single-row comparison operators like equals, greater than, less than, and not equals. This is different from a multi-row subquery that returns many values and requires operators such as IN, ANY, or ALL. The single-row subquery is useful when the comparison depends on a value computed at runtime, such as an average or a maximum. A practical example is filtering employees whose salary is greater than the company average: the inner query computes AVG(salary) and returns one value; the outer query compares each salary to that single result. A common misconception is thinking the database will implicitly reduce multiple rows to one value; it will not. If the subquery returns multiple rows, Oracle raises ORA-01427. Another misconception is that scalar subqueries in the SELECT list behave like constant expressions; if they reference the outer query they are correlated and may execute per row. Takeaway: treat single-row subqueries as a one-by-one value provider and validate the inner query returns exactly one value before relying on it.

Understanding the execution order clarifies why an inner calculation can drive an outer comparison. Oracle evaluates the subquery first if it does not depend on the outer row, producing a single scalar result. That scalar is then used in the outer WHERE or HAVING comparison as if you had hard-coded the value. For correlated scalar subqueries placed in the SELECT list, the inner query references the outer row and therefore executes once per outer row; this produces a contextual value for each returned row. A concrete example is computing the department average inside a correlated subquery in the SELECT list: for every employee row, the inner query computes AVG(salary) for that employee's department. A common misconception is to assume correlated scalars are free — they can be expensive because of repeated execution. Walkthrough steps: 1) Run and inspect the inner query alone to confirm shape. 2) If independent, let the database compute it once and substitute the scalar. 3) If correlated, be aware of the per-row cost and consider a join or analytic function alternative. Reflect: are you getting a single scalar or will the inner logic run many times?

Choosing the right comparison operator stops logic problems before they occur. Single-row operators, such as equals, greater than, and less than, are correct only when the subquery returns one value. If you inadvertently use one of these while the subquery produces multiple rows, Oracle raises ORA-01427. An alternative is to use multiple-row operators: IN compares a value against a set of values, ANY and ALL allow comparisons across sets using relational operators. For example, if a subquery might return several department identifiers, the outer query should use IN instead of equals to match any of those departments. A practical habit is to run the subquery alone, inspect the number of rows, and then select the operator that matches that result shape. A common misconception is thinking that ANY and ALL are interchangeable; they are not. ANY returns true if the comparison is true for at least one value, while ALL requires the comparison to be true for every returned value. Always map the operator semantics to the intended business rule. Single-Row Operators vs. Multiple-Row Alternatives means use single-row operators only with one-value subqueries; use in, any, or all when the subquery can return multiple values.. In practical terms, when to use =, >, < and when to prefer in, any, all. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

ORA-01427 appears when a single-row comparison operator expects one value but the subquery returns multiple rows. The database cannot reduce multiple values to a single scalar automatically, so it reports this error. To diagnose it, run the inner query by itself exactly as written and check the number of rows it returns. If you find more than one row, determine whether to refine the subquery to a single value by adding aggregation, narrowing filters, or by returning a specific key. Alternatively, change the outer comparison to a multiple-row operator like IN, ANY, or ALL to express the intended logic. A concrete example in the chapter shows attempting to match department_id to the department_id of an employee with last name 'King' — if multiple employees share that name and belong to different departments, the subquery returns several department identifiers and ORA-01427 occurs. A common student mistake is trying to fix ORA-01427 by adding LIMIT-like clauses they are unfamiliar with in Oracle; instead, use aggregation, stricter predicates, or the appropriate multi-row operator. Final thought: knowing the shape of your subquery result is the quickest way to avoid this error.

Single-row subqueries also appear in HAVING clauses to filter grouped aggregates. Because HAVING evaluates after GROUP BY computes aggregates, placing a subquery that returns a single value in HAVING lets you compare group aggregates to a calculated reference. A concrete example from the chapter finds departments where the department average salary exceeds the average salary of a specific job role, such as IT programmers. The inner subquery computes AVG(salary) for IT programmers and returns one scalar. The HAVING clause then compares each department's AVG(salary) to that reference. A potential pitfall is forgetting that both sides of the comparison are aggregates: ensure the subquery is scalar and that grouping logic produces one value per department. If the inner subquery accidentally yields multiple rows, ORA-01427 will occur. Another misconception is assuming HAVING can use non-aggregated columns without GROUP BY; it cannot. Takeaway: use single-row subqueries in HAVING to compare group-level aggregates to runtime-computed reference values, and validate the inner query returns one scalar. Using Single-Row Subqueries in HAVING means having can compare a group aggregate to a scalar subquery result; ensure both sides are compatible and scalar.. In practical terms, filtering grouped results with a single scalar comparison. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The inner query uses AVG(salary) to compute that single reference number at runtime. When you run the inner query on its own it returns one numeric result. The outer query then compares each employee's salary to that computed average and returns only those above it. This approach is powerful because the threshold adapts to data changes without rewriting the outer S Q L. A common misconception is to believe this is slower than a precomputed constant; for stable datasets a stored threshold might save time, but the dynamic subquery guarantees correctness. A scalar subquery in the SELECT list returns at most one value per outer row and enriches each result row with contextual information. Often these are correlated: the inner query references a column from the outer row, for example department_id, to compute an aggregate specific to that row's context. An example is adding department average salary alongside each employee row. This is powerful for reporting because each returned row carries its own computed context. However, correlated scalar subqueries may execute once per outer row, which can impact performance on large datasets. A misconception is to overuse scalar subqueries where a join or analytic function would be more efficient.
